parts.article:
The Voynich Manuscript
 
(A) The starkly modern Beinecke Library at Yale University is home to some of the most valuable books in the world: first folios of Shakespeare, Gutenberg Bibles and manuscripts from the early Middle Ages. Yet the library's most controversial possession is an unprepossessing vellum manuscript about the size of a hardback book, containing 240-odd pages of drawings and text of unknown age and authorship. Catalogued as MS 408, the manuscript would attract little attention were it not for the fact that the drawings hint at esoteric knowledge, while the text seems to be some sort of code — one that no-one has been able to break. It is known to scholars as the Voynich manuscript, after the American book-dealer Wilfrid Voynich, who bought the manuscript from a Jesuit college in Italy in 1912. Over the years, the manuscript has attracted the attention of everyone from amateur dabblers to top code-breakers, all determined to succeed where countless others have failed. Academic research papers, books and websites are devoted to making sense of the contents of the manuscript, which are freely available to all. “Most other mysteries involve second-hand reports,” says Dr Gordon Rugg of Keele University, a leading Voynich expert. “But this is one that you can see for yourself.”
 
(B) It is certainly strange: page after page of drawings of weird plants, astrological symbolism and human figures, accompanied by a script that looks like some form of shorthand. What does it say — and what are the drawings about? Voynich himself believed that the manuscript was the work of the 13th-century English monk Roger Bacon, famed for his knowledge of alchemy, philosophy and science. In 1921 Voynich's view that Bacon was the writer appeared to win support from the work of William Newbold, Professor of Philosophy at the University of Pennsylvania, who claimed to have found the key to the cipher system used by Bacon. According to Newbold, the manuscript proved that Bacon had access to a microscope centuries before they were supposedly first invented. The claim that this medieval monk had observed living cells created a sensation. It soon became clear, however, that Newbold had fallen victim to wishful thinking. Other scholars showed that his “decoding” methods produced a host of possible interpretations.
 
(C) The Voynich manuscript has continued to defy the efforts of world-class experts. In 1944, a team was assembled to tackle the mystery, led by William Friedman, the renowned American code breaker. They began with the most basic code-breaking task: analysing the relative frequencies of the characters making up the text, looking for signs of an underlying structure. Yet Friedman's team soon found themselves in deep water. The precise size of the “alphabet” of the Voynich manuscript was unclear: it is possible to make out more than 70 distinct symbols among the 170,000-character text. Furthermore, Friedman discovered that some words and phrases appeared more often than expected in a standard language, casting doubt on claims that the manuscript concealed a real language, as encryption typically reduces word frequencies. Friedman concluded that the most plausible resolution of this paradox was that “Voynichese” is some sort of specially created artificial language, whose words are devised from concepts rather than linguistics. So could the Voynich manuscript be the earliest-known example of an artificial language? “Friedman's hypothesis commands respect because of the lifetime of cryptanalytic expertise he brought to bear,” says Rob Churchill, co-author of The Voynich Manuscript. That still leaves a host of questions unanswered, however, such as the identity of the author and the meaning of the bizarre drawings. “It does little to advance our understanding of the manuscript as a whole,” says Churchill.
 
(D) Even though Friedman was working more than 60 years ago, he suspected that major insights would come from using the device that had already transformed code-breaking: the computer. In this he was right — it is now the key tool for uncovering clues about the manuscript's language. The insights so far have been perplexing. For example, in 2001 another leading Voynich scholar, Dr Gabriel Landini of Birmingham University in the UK, published the results of his study of the manuscript using a pattern-detecting method called spectral analysis. This revealed evidence that the manuscript contains genuine words, rather than random nonsense, consistent with the existence of some underlying natural language. Yet the following year, Voynich expert René Zandbergen of the European Space Agency in Darmstadt, Germany, showed that the entropy of the text (a measure of the rate of transfer of information) was consistent with Friedman's suspicions that an artificial language had been used.
 
(E) Many are convinced that the Voynich manuscript is not a hoax. For how could a medieval hoaxer create so many tell-tale signs of a message from random nonsense? Yet even this has been challenged in new research by Rugg. Using a system first published by the Italian mathematician Girolamo Cardano in 1150, in which a specially constructed grille is used to pick out symbols from a table, Rugg found he could rapidly generate text with many of the basic traits of the Voynich manuscript. Publishing his results in 2004, Rugg stresses that he had not set out to prove the manuscript a hoax. “I simply demonstrated that it is feasible to hoax something this complex in a few months,” he says.
 
(F) Inevitably, others beg to differ. Some scholars, such as Zandbergen, still suspect the text has genuine meaning, though believe it may never be decipherable. Others, such as Churchill, have suggested that the sheer weirdness of the illustrations and text hints at an author who had lost touch with reality. What is clear is that the book-sized manuscript, kept under lock and key at Yale University, has lost none of its fascination. “Many derive great intellectual pleasure from solving puzzles,” says Rugg. “The Voynich manuscript is as challenging a puzzle as anyone could ask for.”

Q40 The writer's main aim in this passage is to

reference:
Q27

干扰 “Uncertain when... written” 对应原文的 “unknown age”。

句子 (Paragraph A) “...containing 240-odd pages of drawings and text of unknown age and authorship.”

解析 题目说伏尼契手稿的写作时间是不确定的。原文A段说这本手稿包含240多页的图画和“of unknown age and authorship（未知年代和作者的）”文字，即时间不确定，选 TRUE。

Q28

解析 题目说Wilfrid Voynich把手稿捐赠给了Beinecke图书馆。原文A段只说他在1912年买了手稿，现在手稿在耶鲁大学图书馆，但并未提及是他“donated（捐赠）”的，中间过程缺失，选 NOT GIVEN。

干扰 不要脑补“他在哪买的”和“现在在哪”中间的环节，文中未提捐赠行为。

句子 (Paragraph A) “...Wilfrid Voynich, who bought the manuscript... in 1912.” (No mention of donation)

Q29

解析 题目说对手稿的兴趣超出了学者和专业破译者。原文A段说多年来它吸引了“everyone from amateur dabblers to top code-breakers（从业余爱好者到顶级破译者）”，即不仅限于专业人士，选 TRUE。

干扰 “Extends beyond” 对应原文的 “everyone from... to...”。

句子 (Paragraph A) “Over the years, the manuscript has attracted the attention of everyone from amateur dabblers to top code-breakers...”

Q30

干扰 数量关系：more than 70 ≠ just under 70。

解析 题目说手稿包含略少于70个符号。原文C段说可能辨认出“more than 70 distinct symbols（超过70个独特符号）”，题目说“just under（略少于）”，直接矛盾，选 FALSE。

句子 (Paragraph C) “It is possible to make out more than 70 distinct symbols among the 170,000-character text.”

Q31

解析 题目说某些词出现的次数使得手稿不太可能基于一种真实的语言。原文C段 Friedman 发现某些词和短语出现的频率比标准语言中预期的要高（appeared more often），这让人怀疑手稿隐藏了真实语言，选 D。

干扰 “Number of times... occur” 对应 “frequencies... appeared more often”，“unlikely... authentic language” 对应 “casting doubt on... concealed a real language”。

句子 (Paragraph C) “Friedman discovered that some words and phrases appeared more often than expected... casting doubt on claims that the manuscript concealed a real language...”

Q32

解析 题目说与其他类似令人着迷的物品不同，人们可以直接接触伏尼契手稿。原文A段末尾 Gordon Rugg 说大多数其他谜团涉及二手报告，但这一个是“you can see for yourself（你可以亲眼看到的）”，即可以直接接触，选 A。

干扰 “Direct access” 对应 “see for yourself”。

句子 (Paragraph A) “...says Dr Gordon Rugg... 'But this is one that you can see for yourself.'”

Q33

句子 (Paragraph F) “Others, such as Churchill, have suggested that... hints at an author who had lost touch with reality.”

解析 题目说写手稿的人可能并不完全理智（sane）。原文F段 Churchill 认为插图和文字的怪异暗示作者可能“lost touch with reality（与现实脱节/精神失常）”，选 E。

干扰 “Not been entirely sane” 对应 “lost touch with reality”。

Q34

解析 题目说手稿作者很可能就是Wilfrid Voynich所建议的那个人。原文B段提到Voynich认为作者是Roger Bacon，而在1921年，William Newbold 的工作似乎支持了这一观点（win support），即他也认为作者是Bacon，选 C。

干扰 Voynich 建议是 Bacon，Newbold 支持这一观点，即 Newbold 同意 Voynich 的建议。

句子 (Paragraph B) “...Voynich himself believed... work of Roger Bacon... win support from the work of William Newbold...”

Q35

解析 题目说Newbold认为作者能够通过____观察细胞。原文B段提到Newbold声称手稿证明Bacon拥有“microscope（显微镜）”并观察了活细胞，填 microscope。

干扰 “Look at cells through a...” 对应原文的 “access to a microscope... observed living cells”。

句子 (Paragraph B) “...manuscript proved that Bacon had access to a microscope... observed living cells...”

Q36

解析 题目说Friedman总结手稿是用一种基于____的人造语言写的。原文C段提到Friedman认为这是一种人造语言，其词汇是设计自“concepts（概念）”而非语言学，填 concepts。

干扰 “Based on” 对应原文的 “devised from”。

句子 (Paragraph C) “...artificial language, whose words are devised from concepts rather than linguistics.”

Q37

干扰 题目中的 “bring advances” 对应原文的 “major insights would come from”。

解析 一句话正确答案解析： 题目说他相信____将继续带来破译进展。原文D段提到Friedman怀疑主要见解将来自使用“the computer（计算机）”，填computer。

句子 (Paragraph D) “...he suspected that major insights would come from using... the computer.”

Q38

解析 题目说Landini使用了一种被称为____的系统。原文D段提到Landini使用了一种名为“spectral analysis（光谱分析）”的模式检测方法，填 spectral analysis。

干扰 “System known as” 对应原文的 “method called”。

句子 (Paragraph D) “...using a pattern-detecting method called spectral analysis.”

Q39

解析 题目说Rugg的系统涉及一个格栅，可以快速选择出现在____中的符号。原文E段提到使用格栅从“table（表格）”中挑选符号，填 table。

干扰 “Select symbols that appeared in a” 对应原文的 “pick out symbols from a”。

句子 (Paragraph E) “...a specially constructed grille is used to pick out symbols from a table...”

Q40

解析 题目问作者在本文的主要目的。通读全文，文章依次介绍了Newbold、Friedman、Landini、Zandbergen、Rugg等多位研究者的尝试和理论，展示了“numerous attempts（众多尝试）”来破译手稿，并未给出最终确定的含义或作者，对应选项 C。

干扰 A（解释含义）和 B（确定作者）都未在文中实现（至今未解）；D（媒体报道）非重点。文章主线是“回顾破译历程”。
